Rights advocates report 23 prisoner deaths during heatwave in Tunisia
In Tunisia, at least 23 prisoners have died in recent weeks due to extreme heat, rights advocates say. According to Asharq Al-Awsat, the Tunisian League for Human Rights (LTDH) links the deaths to high temperatures and detention conditions in overcrowded prisons.
LTDH president Bassam Trifi told AFP that the organization documented 23 deaths based on information from doctors, lawyers and relatives of those who died in prison. According to him, temperatures in overcrowded cells sometimes exceeded 45 degrees Celsius during the heatwave.
The position of authorities and rights advocates
Tunisian authorities have not yet released statistics on prison deaths for the summer. One official said that a death can be linked to heat only after a conclusion by forensic experts.
Human rights organizations have long criticized conditions in Tunisian prisons because of chronic overcrowding, insufficient ventilation and limited access to water. The prison administration has rejected these accusations. In July, it stated that all prisoners receive medical care in accordance with the rules and that necessary measures had been taken in response to the heat.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
The World Organisation Against Torture expressed concern over deteriorating detention conditions and a rising number of prison deaths. It called for transparent and independent investigations and asked authorities to allow human rights groups to visit prisons. LTDH said that its representatives have been barred from such visits since November 2025.
Concerns over imprisoned critics of the president
Relatives of imprisoned critics of President Kais Saied have also voiced concerns about detention conditions during the summer heat. Among them is 85-year-old Ennahdha party leader Rached Ghannouchi. His lawyers called the politician's health condition critical in July following reports of fainting and severe exhaustion.
The daughter of 82-year-old activist Ahmed Nejib Chebbi expressed concern about his detention conditions and those of other prisoners. Her uncle, Issam Chebbi, is also in prison; human rights groups describe the charges against him as politically motivated.
Concern has separately increased over the health of investigative journalist Mohamed Yousfi, who was detained last week before a planned appearance on a radio program about water supply disruptions. He later underwent surgery for appendicitis. The National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists said members of his defense had to leave an interrogation to bring him medication.

title: Heat stroke is threat to stars’ health – and lives - The Observer

full_text:
Perhaps you saw the meme going around during the peak summer heatwave of a person holding up a placard with the message: “Welcome to the coldest summer of the rest of your life (by the way).”
The Met Office confirmed this month that the summer of 2026 was the hottest on record in the UK, looking at data going back to 1884. For the first time ever, a temperature of 37C or higher was recorded on three separate occasions. These heat surges are not one-offs, but part of a pattern. The five hottest summers on record in the UK, determined by the average mean temperature during the day and overnight, have occurred since 2003. The top two came in 2026 (16.5C) and 2025 (16.1C). The famed heatwave of 1976 is now languishing in seventh place.
It is important to stress that changes to climate are not solely heat-related. The Met Office said on Friday that “wetter than average conditions” are now expected this autumn, as the pendulum swings from one extreme to the other.
From a sporting context, this new era of extremely hot summers is forcing governing bodies, sports scientists and team managers to reassess how their athletes perform and train during the increasingly testing period between June and August. A section of the Football Association’s medical FAQs is devoted to managing training in extreme weather, warning that “players are at risk of suffering from heat-stress disorders such as heat cramps, heat exhaustion or heat strokes”.
The effects of heat exhaustion or heat stroke in particular can be severe. Last month a rugby player in Japan, Saimoni Vunilagi, died from suspected heat stroke after a training session for his club, Kyuden Voltex. Vunilagi, 26, collapsed after training and died four days later. The temperature in Fukuoka on that Monday reached 35C, with local authorities at the time issuing warnings for extreme heat. The average humidity level in Fukuoka in August is also an oppressive 74%.
Jo Clubb, a sports scientist who runs Global Performance Insights, has previously spent years working with Chelsea FC and the Buffalo Bills in the NFL. Ensuring that elite athletes avoid dehydration is a primary concern.
“At around 2-3% [loss] of your body mass in fluid is when you start to have impaired physiological performance from dehydration,” Clubb says. “In team sports we’re educating the players on not just fluid intake, but also electrolytes, because we don’t want to just be consuming water alone.”
Players running around in full equipment and pads in the NFL naturally sweat more due to that extra exertion. Sweating is essential, as Clubb explains, because the “evaporation of that fluid from the skin then is a mechanism to help us dissipate heat”.
However, sweat loss produces its own issues. “The heart is pumping harder in a heat environment to try and both maintain the blood flow in order to maintain the cardiac output for everything the muscle needs, but equally, some of that fluid is being lost through sweat. So it can be a little bit of a double whammy, having dehydration in a hot environment particularly.”
While the physical exertion elite athletes go through is easy to spot – the sweat, collapsing over a finish line or at the final whistle, or the sight of elite players battling to cool themselves down, such as former France forward Antoine Griezmann recently while playing for MLS side Orlando City – Clubb highlights that the mental toll playing in the heat is just as big a threat, particularly when it comes to picking up injuries.

“Perhaps there’s more cognitive demand, and more demand overall on the body, so the brain is working even harder, in a way, to solve this problem of heat stress,” she adds. “Potentially, dehydration may have got to the level that influences cognitive performance and it may be limiting their concentration.
“There might also be greater risks of injury from, essentially, a poor decision that might put them into a bad position, or just put themselves into a riskier scenario, whether that’s making a tackle that they shouldn’t have made, or not landing well from a header, or the increased risk of those kinds of injuries where it’s hard to say that it’s down to one thing or the other. It’s this whole melting pot of both higher physical and cognitive demand in those kinds of environments.”
The key to recovery, along with rehydration and nutrition, comes through cooling down the body. Hence the popularity – or perhaps unpopularity among athletes – of ice baths after training. England’s rugby players are usually straight into pitchside tubs after hot training sessions at their Pennyhill Park base. Air conditioning businesses may now be booming but the UK has a way to go to catch up to other traditionally warm countries, which can affect both athletes’ immediate recovery and their sleep.
For sports scientists and physiologists, Clubb suggests that the entire nature of their role has changed. No longer are they merely trying to find strategies to ensure that their athletes are “in the best position to succeed” and “trying to get a competitive advantage”. There is an onus to keep them safe.
“It’s a medical aspect,” she says. “It’s a discussion that requires safeguards to be put in place to protect the athletes. And that needs greater governance, obviously, because of the even greater consequences that we’re talking about in those situations.”
For triathletes training at the open-water swimming venue at Six Hills, near Melton Mowbray, discussions in the past during hot weather would centre on removing wetsuits to avoid overheating. This summer at the lake they faced a different dilemma, as explained by Ben Scott, a physiologist for British Triathlon & Para Triathlon at the UK Sports Institute: sections of the lake were drying out.
“We got to a point where people were almost touching the bottom of the floor when they were swimming,” Scott says. “That did get pretty shallow and probably quite close to the point where we’d have to stop going there.”
Acclimatising for triathlons in hot countries is a fairly standard process. This year, however, Scott observed two things: that events held in France and Spain were “really hot races over 30 degrees, with quite warm water as well for the swim components” – and that instead of triathletes simply acclimatising for a couple of races, “it’s now getting to the point where almost every race you’re doing is hot”. He adds: “I’ve had discussions recently about rather than trying to acclimatise for a particular race, doing acclimatisation earlier on and then just trying to maintain it with some top-ups throughout the rest of the year.”
An underappreciated group in these scenarios is spectators. The sight of tennis fans at Wimbledon succumbing to the heat and fainting has become a more regular occurrence in recent years.
In the US, supporters have been abandoning their seats in the upper decks of stadiums that have no protection from the sun in the early weeks of the new college football season, heading to either the concourse or other areas of the stadium to find shade. Calls for games to be played at night only during the early part of the season are increasing.
The constant across all of those groups of people, from sport scientists and physiologists to athletes, organisations and supporters, is that climate change is forcing everyone to adapt throughout the summer months. Now to see what the autumn and winter will bring.

As forecast by the weather department, a spell of heavy rain has begun across the state with the onset of Bhadarva. Between 6 a.m. on September 12 and 6 a.m. on September 13, rainfall was recorded in 193 talukas. Ukai in Tapi recorded the highest rainfall at 12 inches, followed by 8.5 inches in Umarpada, Surat.
84 talukas receive rain in two hours
Between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. on September 13, rainfall was recorded in 84 talukas. Dediapada and Vagra received more than 1.5 inches, the highest rainfall recorded during this two-hour period, while 18 talukas received more than half an inch.
Heavy to extremely heavy rain forecast in Navsari, Valsad
After a long gap, more than 100 talukas in central and south Gujarat received rain on Saturday (12 Sept). However, Saurashtra-Kutch continues to remain largely dry, with farmers waiting for rainfall.
The Meteorological Department has forecast heavy to extremely heavy rain today, issuing a red alert for two districts, an orange alert for six districts and a yellow alert for 12 districts.
State receives 75% of season’s average rainfall
The state has received 75% of its average seasonal rainfall so far. However, 25 districts are still facing rainfall deficits ranging from 1% to 88%.
With heavy rain forecast across the state over the next two days, there are hopes that the rainfall deficit will be reduced.

Heavy rain likely in Punjab till Sep 17; Yellow alert issued
Babushahi Network
Chandigarh, September 13, 2026: Punjab is likely to receive heavy rainfall at some places from Sunday, September 13, through September 17, with the Meteorological Department issuing a yellow alert for the state. Chandigarh is also likely to witness cloudy weather and rain during this period.
The maximum temperature in Punjab fell by 0.5 degrees Celsius on Saturday but remained 1.8 degrees above normal. The highest temperature was recorded at Bhakra Dam at 36.3 degrees Celsius, while Chandigarh recorded 36.8 degrees Celsius, making it warmer than all districts of Punjab.
Rain likely in 16 districts today
According to the Meteorological Department, rain is likely at several places in 16 districts of Punjab on Sunday. Heavy rainfall is possible at isolated places in Pathankot, while light to moderate rain is expected in Gurdaspur, Amritsar, Hoshiarpur, Nawanshahr, Rupnagar and Mohali.
Rain is also likely at some places in Tarn Taran, Kapurthala, Jalandhar, Ludhiana, Barnala, Mansa, Sangrur, Fatehgarh Sahib and Patiala.
Punjab recorded 0.6 mm of rainfall on Saturday. The fresh spell could help reduce the rainfall deficit in several districts during the monsoon season.
Western Disturbance active over North Punjab
A Western Disturbance is currently active over North Punjab and adjoining areas. The cyclonic circulation over North Pakistan and the adjoining Jammu region is now positioned at an altitude of around 3.1 to 5.8 km over North Punjab and neighbouring areas.
The weather system is expected to increase rainfall and cloud cover across the region over the next few days.
Power demand crosses 13,000 MW
Meanwhile, rising heat and humidity have pushed up electricity demand in Punjab. The state’s power demand reached 13,083 MW at 6:30 am on Sunday.
Punjab’s own power generation stood at 4,339 MW, while 8,746 MW was being sourced from the grid. The demand is expected to rise further during the day.
